conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you.  

Today we’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and mentally during the past seven days of this postpartum period. It isn’t a test of your parenting or character; it’s just one of the best ways we have to be sure we’re giving you the right support.  

Everything you share here is confidential. Our goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can be completely honest—there are no “wrong” answers, only the ones that reflect your true experience. The EPDS has ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally rather than reading them off a sheet. We’ll take it at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification at any time.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:  

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things—like a warm drink, a favorite song, or your baby’s smile—or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I still smile when my little guy grips my finger, but even that feels… dimmed. I’ll make myself a cup of tea and think, “This used to taste comforting,” yet it’s mostly just warm water now. So, no, I’m not getting the little lifts I used to—maybe a flicker, but nothing like before.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I’ll hear my husband try to joke or see something silly on my phone and I might force a little “ha,” but it feels fake. Mostly I just feel flat, like I’m too tired or heavy inside to actually laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hardly at all. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a shower without the baby monitor going off—but now it all feels like one more chore. I’ll tell myself “tomorrow might be better,” but I don’t actually believe it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If he spits up more than usual, I immediately think, “Must be something I ate,” or if he’s fussy, I’m sure it’s because I’m not soothing him right. Even when the diaper leaks I catch myself thinking, “A good mom would’ve changed him sooner." It’s like every hiccup feels like my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind’ll just start racing—what if he stops breathing in the bassinet, what if I trip on the stairs and drop him, what if I’m too out-of-it to notice something’s wrong. There’s no real trigger; the worries just show up and circle for hours unless I pace the hallway or check him ten times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, several times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air—like I’m about to get bad news, only there’s no actual danger. It usually passes if I rock the baby or do the breathing video my nurse showed me, but it’s happened three or four nights this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly yes. I feel like I’m wading through wet cement—every little task, folding a onesie or answering a text, just piles on. I’m not falling apart, but I’m definitely running on fumes and snapping at the dog when he barks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. After the night feeds, when the baby’s finally asleep, my brain won’t shut off. I lie there listening to every little grunt he makes, or replaying everything I think I did wrong that day, and it can take an hour or more to drift off—then I jolt awake an hour later with the same worries.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day, but this heavy sadness sits on my chest the minute I open my eyes. Even when I’m doing something “normal,” like folding his laundry, I feel like I’m moving through fog—just dull and weepy inside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice since last weekend. Once was when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was starving him; the other time was after a phone call with my mom—she asked how I was doing and I just cracked. So not every day, but the tears come when the pressure builds.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…Yes, it has, a couple of times. Nothing planned—just these quick, scary flashes, like “what if I weren’t here anymore.” They leave me shaken, because I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thoughts still popped in, maybe twice this week.

You've shared that the small sparks of joy you once felt have nearly gone out: laughter feels forced, simple pleasures like tea taste like warm water, and even your baby's grip brings only a dim smile. Each day brings a heavy, fog-like sadness, racing worries about <sym>harm coming to your son</sym>, <sym>panic episodes</sym> that make your heart pound, and nights spent lying awake replaying every parenting moment you blame yourself for. Twice this week frightening <sym>thoughts of not wanting to be here</sym> have flashed through your mind, leaving you shaken and exhausted.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to genuinely laugh, feeling flat and forcing fake responses, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame for routine infant issues (spitting up, fussiness, diaper leaks), indicating this occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, racing worries without external triggers, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys frequent difficulty coping ('mostly yes,' 'running on fumes'), matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by persistent unhappiness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts twice this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places you well above the ≥14 cut-off that signals probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with immediate safety implications because <sym>item-10≥1</sym>. You described nearly every core symptom required by <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>self-reproach/guilt</sym>, recurrent <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, <sym>sleep-onset insomnia</sym> driven by ruminations, and <sym>fatigue</sym>. Passive suicidal ideation without plan heightens risk. This pattern strongly correlates with moderate-to-severe <med>PPD</med> often complicated by <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day mental-health evaluation or emergency department visit to address self-harm thoughts
2. Contact your <med>primary care provider</med> or local <med>perinatal psychiatry crisis line</med> for immediate safety planning
3. Enlist partner/family to stay with you and baby until professional help is secured
4. Limit isolation-have supportive adult present during high-stress times
5. Practice 5-minute paced breathing when <sym>panic</sym> begins; keep baby in safe place while you breathe
6. Postpone major household tasks; focus only on basic infant care while awaiting treatment
7. Schedule follow-up within 24-48 h to monitor mood, safety, and response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 3 mo post-delivery (per chart)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter or anticipation of pleasure  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy sadness,” tearfulness 2× this week  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety, racing thoughts, somatic tension  
- Multiple panic spells (HR, dyspnea) without clear trigger  
- Sleep-onset insomnia after night feeds linked to ruminations  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed; irritability  
- Passive self-harm thoughts x2 this week (no plan or intent)

Pattern  
All 10 EPDS items positive for clinically significant distress; severity highest for mood, anxiety, and self-harm items.

Screening significance  
- Meets screening cut-off for major postpartum depressive symptoms and comorbid anxiety.  
- Passive suicidal ideation present → immediate safety risk.

Risk factors  
- Guilt / worthfulness cognitions  
- Panic-level physiological arousal  
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood rather than infant care alone

Next step  
Urgent safety assessment and referral to perinatal mental health specialist / crisis team as indicated.
